dialogues.title: Meeting and Introducing Yourself
dialogues.scene: Two people meet for the first time at a language center and introduce themselves in formal Arabic.

lines.speaker: سامي
lines.ref: Peace be upon you (hello).

lines.speaker: لَيْلى
lines.ref: And peace be upon you. Welcome.

lines.speaker: سامي
lines.ref: My name is Sami. What is your name?

lines.speaker: لَيْلى
lines.ref: My name is Layla. Nice to meet you.

lines.speaker: سامي
lines.ref: Where are you from?

lines.speaker: لَيْلى
lines.ref: I am from Lebanon. And you?

lines.speaker: سامي
lines.target: أَنا مِنْ مِصْر. لِماذا تَتَعَلَّمينَ العَرَبيّةَ؟
lines.ref: I am from Egypt. Why are you learning Arabic?

lines.speaker: لَيْلى
lines.ref: I love the Arabic language and culture.

lines.speaker: سامي
lines.ref: Wonderful! I wish you success.

lines.speaker: لَيْلى
lines.ref: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

vocab: سُرِرْتُ بِلِقائِك surirtu bi-liqāʾik (nice to meet you)
dialogues.note: Arabs often ask 'where are you from?' early in a conversation; it signals genuine interest, not intrusion. The reply al-ḥamdu lillāh ('praise God') is expected to 'how are you?' regardless of your actual mood.

dialogues.title: At a Middle Eastern Restaurant
dialogues.scene: A customer orders mezze, a main dish, and tea, then asks for the bill.

lines.speaker: النّادِل
lines.ref: Good evening. Please, come in.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: Good evening. The menu, please.

lines.speaker: النّادِل
lines.ref: Here you are. What would you like to order?

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: I want hummus and a salad to start.

lines.speaker: النّادِل
lines.ref: And after that?

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: Chicken with rice, please.

lines.speaker: النّادِل
lines.ref: And what will you drink?

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: Tea with mint, thank you.

lines.speaker: النّادِل
lines.ref: Right away. Enjoy your meal.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: It was delicious. The bill, please.

dialogues.note: Mint tea (شاي بالنعناع) is a symbol of hospitality across the Arab world. Refusing an offered drink can seem impolite — accepting even a small glass honours the host.

dialogues.title: Asking for Directions in Cairo
dialogues.scene: A visitor stops a passer-by to find a mosque and then a bank.

lines.speaker: الزّائِر
lines.ref: Excuse me, where is the nearby mosque?

lines.speaker: المارّ
lines.ref: Walk straight ahead then turn right.

lines.speaker: الزّائِر
lines.ref: Is it far from here?

lines.speaker: المارّ
lines.target: لا، عَلى بُعْدِ خَمْسِ دَقائِقَ سَيْراً.
lines.ref: No, about five minutes on foot.

lines.speaker: الزّائِر
lines.ref: Thank you. And where is the nearest bank?

lines.speaker: المارّ
lines.ref: The bank is next to the mosque, on the left.

lines.speaker: الزّائِر
lines.ref: Excellent. And how do I get a taxi?

lines.speaker: المارّ
lines.ref: There are taxis in front of the bank.

lines.speaker: الزّائِر
lines.ref: Thank you very much for your help.

lines.speaker: المارّ
lines.ref: You're welcome. Goodbye.

dialogues.note: Egyptians are famously warm with lost strangers and may walk you part of the way rather than just point. Adding min faḍlik or law samaḥt to any request softens it and is always appreciated.

dialogues.title: Bargaining at the Souk
dialogues.scene: A shopper asks about a handmade item and negotiates the price at a market.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: How much is this leather bag?

lines.speaker: البائِع
lines.ref: Two hundred pounds, and it's handmade.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: It's a bit expensive. Any discount?

lines.speaker: البائِع
lines.target: لَكَ سِعْرٌ خاصّ: مِئةٌ وسَبْعونَ جُنَيْهاً.
lines.ref: A special price for you: a hundred and seventy pounds.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: A hundred and fifty, and I'll take it right away.

lines.speaker: البائِع
lines.ref: Agreed. It's yours.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: Excellent! I'll pay in cash.

lines.speaker: البائِع
lines.ref: Thank you. Here is your change.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: The quality is wonderful. Thank you.

lines.speaker: البائِع
lines.ref: You're welcome. Come back to us again.

dialogues.note: Haggling in a souk is expected and friendly, not confrontational — starting near half the asking price is normal. Sharing tea while negotiating is common and does not obligate you to buy.

dialogues.title: A Phone Call to Arrange a Meeting
dialogues.scene: Two colleagues phone to set the time, place, and agenda for a meeting.

lines.speaker: خالِد
lines.target: آلو، مَساءُ الخَيْر يا أُسْتاذ نادِر.
lines.ref: Hello, good evening, Mr. Nader.

lines.speaker: نادِر
lines.target: مَساءُ النّور يا خالِد. كَيْفَ حالُك؟
lines.ref: Good evening, Khalid. How are you?

lines.speaker: خالِد
lines.target: بِخَيْر، شُكْراً. أُريدُ أَنْ نُحَدِّدَ مَوْعِدَ الاجْتِماع.
lines.ref: Fine, thanks. I'd like us to set the meeting time.

lines.speaker: نادِر
lines.ref: Alright. Does Tuesday suit you?

lines.speaker: خالِد
lines.ref: Yes, at ten in the morning.

lines.speaker: نادِر
lines.ref: Excellent. Where will we meet?

lines.speaker: خالِد
lines.ref: In the company office on the third floor.

lines.speaker: نادِر
lines.ref: And what are the main topics?

lines.speaker: خالِد
lines.ref: The new budget and the marketing plan.

lines.speaker: نادِر
lines.target: اتَّفَقْنا. سَأُؤَكِّدُ الحُضورَ بِرِسالةٍ. إلى اللِّقاء.
lines.ref: Agreed. I'll confirm attendance by message. See you.

dialogues.note: In professional Arabic, addressing someone as أُستاذ (ustādh, 'professor/sir') plus their first name is a common mark of respect. Business often opens with a brief exchange about health and family before turning to the agenda.

dialogues.title: At the Pharmacy
dialogues.scene: A customer describes symptoms and asks the pharmacist for medicine and instructions.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: Peace be upon you. I have a headache and a fever.

lines.speaker: الصَّيْدَليّ
lines.target: وعَلَيْكُمُ السَّلام. مُنْذُ مَتى تَشْعُرُ بِذٰلِك؟
lines.ref: And peace be upon you. Since when have you felt this?

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: For two days, and I feel tired too.

lines.speaker: الصَّيْدَليّ
lines.target: هَلْ عِنْدَكَ حَساسيّةٌ مِنْ أَيِّ دَواء؟
lines.ref: Do you have an allergy to any medicine?

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: No, I don't think so.

lines.speaker: الصَّيْدَليّ
lines.target: خُذْ هٰذا الدَّواءَ حَبّةً كُلَّ ثَماني ساعات.
lines.ref: Take this medicine, one tablet every eight hours.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.target: هَلْ آخُذُهُ قَبْلَ الأَكْلِ أَمْ بَعْدَه؟
lines.ref: Do I take it before eating or after?

lines.speaker: الصَّيْدَليّ
lines.ref: After eating, and drink plenty of water.

lines.speaker: الزَّبون
lines.ref: And if the fever continues?

lines.speaker: الصَّيْدَليّ
lines.ref: See a doctor. Get well soon.

dialogues.note: Pharmacies in many Arab countries dispense a wide range of medicines without a prescription, and the pharmacist is often the first port of call for minor ailments. سَلامَتُك (salāmatuk) is the warm standard way to wish a sick person well; the reply is Allāh yusallimak.
